Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and time orientation given by increasing $x^0$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$; it is off shell, meaning that it is not required to satisfy a field equation. For an integer $s\ge0$, its finite jet at $x$ is the finite tuple $j^s\phi(x)=(\partial^\alpha\phi(x))_{|\alpha|\le s}$, with multi-index derivatives in these coordinates.

An off-shell local polynomial scalar functional is a finite sum
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{a=1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb M} f_a(x)\,P_a(j^{s_a}\phi(x))\,d^4x,$$
where $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$, each $P_a$ is a polynomial in the finitely many jet coordinates, and each $s_a$ is finite. Its support is contained in the compact set $\bigcup_{a=1}^{N}\operatorname{supp}f_a$. The collection of these functionals is denoted $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$. The involution is $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$. No physical units or field equation are imposed.

Precisely, $\operatorname{supp}F$ is the set of $x\in\mathbb M$ such that every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains the support of some $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ for which $F(\phi+h)\ne F(\phi)$ for some smooth configuration $\phi$. It is closed and is contained in the displayed compact union, so it is compact. This definition is independent of the chosen finite presentation of $F$.

For $r\ge1$, define the $r$th functional derivative by
$$F^{(r)}(\phi)(h_1,\ldots,h_r)=\left.\frac{\partial^r}{\partial t_1\cdots\partial t_r}F\!\left(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^{r}t_jh_j\right)\right|_{t_1=\cdots=t_r=0},\qquad h_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R).$$
The finite polynomial expansion makes this a symmetric multilinear form. Repeated integration by parts in each $h_j$ writes it as a compactly supported distribution kernel on the thin diagonal $\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathbb M\}\subset\mathbb M^r$. Integrals use the fixed Minkowski density $d^4x$; all kernels are paired bilinearly with compactly supported smooth tests.

Let $\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ be open and let $u\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$, using the local distribution convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. For $p\in\Omega$ and $\xi\in\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, call $(p,\xi)$ regular for $u$ if there are $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $\chi=1$ near $p$ and an open cone $\Gamma\subseteq\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$ containing $\xi$ such that for every integer $N\ge0$,
$$ \sup_{\eta\in\Gamma}(1+|\eta|)^N\left|\left\langle u,\chi(x)e^{-2\pi i x\cdot\eta}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|\right\rangle\right|<\infty. $$
The local wavefront set $\operatorname{WF}_\Omega(u)$ is the complement of these regular pairs in $T^*\Omega\setminus0$, with the standard cotangent coordinates $(p,\xi)$. A cone is invariant under multiplication by positive scalars. This is a chart-level definition; this item makes no assertion about its behavior under a change of coordinates.

Let $M$ be an oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$, with signature $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. A cotangent vector is future or past causal when its metric dual belongs to the corresponding closed causal tangent cone. For $r\ge1$, let $\overline V_\pm^r\subset T^*M^r\setminus0$ consist of tuples $(x_1,\ldots,x_r;\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r)$ such that every $\xi_j$ is either zero or future causal for $+$, respectively past causal for $-$, and the total tuple is nonzero. The wavefront set used below is the set of nonzero cotangent tuples where compactly localized Fourier transforms fail rapid decay in every conic neighborhood.

A compactly supported polynomial functional is a finite expression
$$ F(\phi)=\sum_{m=0}^{N}\left\langle f_m,\phi^{\otimes m}\mu_g^{\otimes m}\right\rangle, $$
where $\phi\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$, $f_m\in\mathcal E'(M^m)$ is symmetric under permutations of its $m$ variables, $\mu_g$ is the metric density fixed by the Lorentzian metric, and the pairing is defined by inserting a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}f_m$ in the smooth factor. Its $r$th functional derivative $F^{(r)}(\phi)\in\mathcal E'(M^r)$ is specified, for a test density $\omega$ on $M^r$, by
$$ \left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi),\omega\right\rangle =\sum_{m=r}^{N}\frac{m!}{(m-r)!} \left\langle f_m,\omega\otimes\phi^{\otimes(m-r)}\mu_g^{\otimes(m-r)}\right\rangle, $$
where a compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}f_m$ is inserted in the smooth $\phi$ factors. Expanding the finite polynomial shows that this kernel represents the directional derivative in smooth compactly supported real directions. The functional is microcausal when
$$ \operatorname{WF}(F^{(r)}(\phi))\cap(\overline V_+^r\cup\overline V_-^r)=\varnothing $$
for every $r\ge1$ and every $\phi\in C^\infty(M;\mathbb R)$. Write $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)$ for this class, including constants.

Let $(M,g)$ be a Hausdorff, second-countable, oriented, time-oriented, globally hyperbolic smooth Lorentzian $n$-manifold without boundary, $n\ge2$. Here $g$ is a smooth symmetric nondegenerate bilinear form on each tangent space with one negative and $n-1$ positive directions; in charts its signature is $(-,+,\ldots,+)$. An orientation is a smooth choice of orientation in each tangent space. A time orientation selects one of the two components of $\{v\ne0:g(v,v)<0\}$ as future. A tangent vector is causal when $g(v,v)\le0$, and is future or past causal when it belongs to the closure of the selected future or past timelike cone. A causal curve is piecewise $C^1$ with causal tangent consistently future or past directed. Put $J^+(p)$ and $J^-(p)$ for the points reached from or reaching $p$ by such curves. Here globally hyperbolic means strongly causal and every causal diamond $J^+(p)\cap J^-(q)$ is compact; strongly causal means every point has arbitrarily small neighborhoods which each causal curve meets in a connected parameter interval. A nonzero cotangent vector is future or past causal, or future or past null, when its metric dual under $g^{-1}$ has the corresponding tangent property.

Let $\nabla$ be the unique torsion-free connection with $\nabla g=0$. Define the smooth metric density $\mu_g=|\det(g_{ab})|^{1/2}|dx^1\cdots dx^n|$ in a chart. It is coordinate-independent: under $y=\psi(x)$, $g_y=(D\psi^{-1})^Tg_xD\psi^{-1}$, so $|\det g_y|^{1/2}=|\det D\psi^{-1}|\,|\det g_x|^{1/2}$, the density transformation law. Functional-kernel pairings and contractions on this page use $\mu_g$ in each integrated variable; no physical units are assigned.

For each smooth chart $x:U\to\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$, let $u_x\in\mathcal D'(\Omega)$ be the coordinate representative of $u$ in the test-density convention of [[def-qftx-distributions-on-smooth-manifolds]]. Map a local covector $(x(p),\xi)\in T^*\Omega$ to $(p,dx_p^T\xi)\in T^*M$. Define the global wavefront set by the union over all charts,
$$ \operatorname{WF}(u):=\bigcup_{(U,x)}\{(p,dx_p^T\xi):(x(p),\xi)\in\operatorname{WF}_{x(U)}(u_x)\}\subset T^*M\setminus0, $$
where the local sets are those of [[def-qftx-local-wavefront-set]]. Thus the global set is defined using all charts; equality of the chartwise descriptions on overlaps is a separate theorem. The Fourier convention is the displayed $2\pi$ convention.

An affinely parametrized null geodesic is a smooth curve $\gamma$ with $g(\dot\gamma,\dot\gamma)=0$ and $\nabla_{\dot\gamma}\dot\gamma=0$; it is future-directed when $\dot\gamma$ lies in the chosen future causal cone. Two nonzero future-null cotangent vectors $(p,\xi)$ and $(q,\zeta)$ are related, written $(p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta)$, if a future-directed affinely parametrized null geodesic from $p$ to $q$ carries $\xi$ to $\zeta$ by the induced parallel transport on covectors; for $p=q$ the zero-length segment has $\zeta=\xi$. Define the positive-frequency null relation
$$ \mathcal C^+_g:=\{(p,\xi;q,-\zeta): (p,\xi)\sim(q,\zeta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}\subset T^*(M\times M)\setminus0. $$
For a fixed scalar second-order operator $P=-g^{ab}\nabla_a\nabla_b+X^a\nabla_a+V$, with smooth vector field $X$, smooth scalar $V$, inverse metric $g^{ab}$, and Levi-Civita derivative $\nabla$, a scalar Hadamard bisolution is a distribution $W\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$ satisfying $P_xW=P_yW=0$ and $\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+_g$. Write $W^{\mathsf T}=\tau^*W$ for the pullback by $\tau(x,y)=(y,x)$. A fixed antisymmetric part means the equality $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for one specified distribution $E$. This definition asserts no existence of $W$ and fixes no field-operator or commutator sign beyond the displayed convention.

derivations.claim: Expand the finite polynomial in the definition of $F$ after substituting $\phi+\sum_jt_jh_j$ and take the coefficient of $t_1\cdots t_r$. Each resulting term has the form $\int a(x)\prod_{j=1}^{r}\partial^{\alpha_j}h_j(x)\,d^4x$ with $a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M)$. Integrating by parts in the compactly supported directions moves every $\partial^{\alpha_j}$ onto the smooth coefficient, so the term becomes $\int b(x)\prod_jh_j(x)\,d^4x$ for a smooth compactly supported $b$. Its distribution kernel on $\mathbb M^r$ is $b(x)\prod_{j<r}\delta(x_j-x_r)$, supported on $\Delta_r$.

In coordinates $x=x_r$ and $z_j=x_j-x_r$ for $j<r$, a compact localization of this kernel is $b_0(x)\prod_{j<r}\delta(z_j)$ with $b_0\in C_c^\infty$. Its Fourier transform in $(x,z)$ is $\widehat b_0(\kappa)$, independent of the normal frequencies $\zeta_j$. Since $\widehat b_0$ is rapidly decreasing in $\kappa$, rapid decay holds in every closed cone where $|\kappa|\ge\epsilon|(\kappa,\zeta)|$ for some $\epsilon>0$. Therefore any wavefront covector has $\kappa=0$, so it is conormal to $\Delta_r$. In the original coordinates this is exactly $\sum_j\xi_j=0$.

If $\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r$ are all future causal covectors in this Minkowski chart, their metric-dual time components have one weak sign, and a nonzero causal covector has a strictly nonzero time component. Thus $\sum_j\xi_j=0$ forces every $\xi_j=0$. The same argument applies to past causal covectors. By step 2.1 the wavefront set is conormal, so it contains no nonzero tuple in either forbidden cone of [F3]. This proves microcausality.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. Use units $c=1$, so a mass parameter has inverse-length units. Define $x\in J^+(y)$ by $x^0-y^0\ge|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|$ and $x\in J^-(y)$ by $y^0-x^0\ge|\mathbf y-\mathbf x|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb M$, put $J^\pm(A)=\bigcup_{y\in A}J^\pm(y)$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. The support of a functional $F$ is the closed set of points each of whose neighborhoods contains the support of a compactly supported variation that changes $F$ for some configuration.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. The proper orthochronous Poincare group consists of $\gamma=(a,\Lambda)$ with $a\in\mathbb M$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$. It acts by $(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ and $(\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi)$.

For a distribution on a coordinate chart, its wavefront set consists of the nonzero cotangent directions where every compact localization fails to have a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform in every conic neighborhood. Covectors are future or past causal when their metric-dual vectors are causal with the indicated time orientation; a nonzero causal covector has a nonzero time component. Write $\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and $N^*\Delta=\{(x,\xi;x,-\xi):\xi\ne0\}$. Write $(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta)$ when $x,y$ lie on one null straight segment (a zero-length segment is allowed), and parallel transport along that segment carries $\xi$ to $\eta$. A fixed free scalar input consists of $m\ge0$, a two-point distribution $W$ satisfying
$$P_xW=P_yW=0,\qquad P=-\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b+m^2,$$
and the positive-frequency null wavefront condition
$$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

The prescribed scalar time-ordered contraction input is a symmetric distribution $H_F\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb M^2)$ invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, equal to $W(x,y)$ on the open set $x^0>y^0$ and to $W(y,x)$ on $y^0>x^0$. The two prescriptions agree on spacelike-separated open supports because $E$ is supported on causal pairs. Translation invariance gives $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ and $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$. For a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^4$, set $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-4}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$ and define $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$ as the infimum of real $\omega$ for which $\rho^\omega T_\rho\to0$ on each fixed test as $\rho\downarrow0$. Require $\operatorname{sd}_0(h_F),\operatorname{sd}_0(w)\le2$ and
$$\operatorname{WF}(H_F)\subseteq\Gamma_F:=N^*\Delta\cup\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):x\ne y,\ (x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null if }x\in J^+(y),\ \xi\text{ past null if }x\in J^-(y)\}.$$
This is fixed conditional data: it does not claim existence of $W$ or $H_F$, and it does not define any singular restriction or product of $H_F$ on a diagonal.

For $r\ge1$, $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ denotes the distribution kernel on $\mathbb M^r$ of the mixed variation in $r$ compactly supported smooth directions, and set $F^{(0)}(\phi)=F(\phi)$. Define $\deg F$ as the largest positive $r$ with $F^{(r)}\ne0$, or $0$ if all positive-order derivative kernels vanish; in particular $\deg0=0$. The class $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$ consists of finite polynomial functionals with compactly supported derivative kernels such that every nonzero wavefront tuple of each derivative kernel avoids both the cone of tuples whose entries are all future causal and the cone of tuples whose entries are all past causal; zero entries in either cone are allowed. For $F,G$ in this class, define
$$F\star_WG=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)}\frac{\hbar^r}{r!}\left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle,$$
using distribution products and pushforwards under the stated wavefront transversality conditions, with the $r=0$ pairing interpreted as the pointwise product $F(\phi)G(\phi)$. Here $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate, and Countable Choice is assumed for the supplier theorem defining these contractions.

A scalar time-ordered system is a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps
$$T_n:\big(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\big)^n\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket,\qquad T_0=1,\quad T_1=\operatorname{id}.$$
For $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ put $S_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{supp}F_i$ and $F_I=(F_i)_{i\in I}$. Causal factorization requires
$$T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=T_{|I|}(F_I)\star_W T_{|I^c|}(F_{I^c})$$
for every nonempty proper $I$ such that $S_I\cap J^-(S_{I^c})=\varnothing$; an empty block is the unit.

Field independence means that each numerical graph distribution is independent of the background field $\phi$; all $\phi$-dependence enters through the vertex kernels $F_i^{(r)}(\phi)$. In the graph expansion of $T_n$, vertices are labeled by $1,\ldots,n$ and an edge between distinct vertices contracts one derivative slot at each endpoint by $H_F$. A graph is a finite loopless multigraph, so parallel edges are allowed; if $r_{ij}$ edges join vertices $i$ and $j$, the Wick coefficient for that choice includes $\hbar^{\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}}/\prod_{i<j}r_{ij}!$. Finite-order local jet derivatives may act on incident edge kernels. Each coefficient is a finite sum of such contractions, since every input has finite polynomial degree. No graph term uses a singular product at a diagonal before extension.

For $n\ge2$, use relative coordinates $z_i=x_i-x_n$ ($1\le i<n$), so the total diagonal corresponds to $0\in\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}$. The relative scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma$ of a numerical graph distribution is defined by the same positive-dilation rule above in this relative dimension. The scaling condition requires each graph distribution on the punctured relative space, after its proper partial diagonals have been extended at lower vertex orders, to have a finite degree $\delta_\Gamma$, and each total-diagonal extension to retain that degree. Any two such extensions differ by derivatives $\partial^\beta\delta_0$ of order $|\beta|\le\lfloor\delta_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $\delta_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and agree when $\delta_\Gamma<4(n-1)$.

Covariance requires $T_n(\gamma\cdot F_1,\ldots,\gamma\cdot F_n)=\gamma\cdot T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ for each proper orthochronous Poincare transformation. Fix the Lorentz Lie-algebra convention $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_j$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_i$. For a formal coupling $g$, define coefficientwise
$$\mathcal S_g(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(ig/\hbar)^n}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
The anti-time-ordered series is $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V):=\mathcal S_g(V)^*$, where the involution conjugates scalar coefficients, fixes real $g,\hbar$, and reverses the order of factors; $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$ gives $(F\star_WG)^*=G^*\star_WF^*$. Formal unitarity requires $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V)\star_W\mathcal S_g(V)=1$ for every real $V=V^*$. At each $g$-order, coefficients are finite Laurent polynomials in $\hbar$ before cancellation and are compared algebraically; there is no analytic convergence, positivity of formal coefficients, adiabatic limit, or gauge/Ward identity in this contract.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

For this fixed $t$, define its **local extension family** by

$$\mathcal E(t):=\{T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n):T|_U=t\}.$$

Here $T|_U=t$ means $\langle T,\widetilde\varphi\rangle=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$, where $\widetilde\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ is its smooth extension by zero. When $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)\in\mathbb R$, the **scaling-degree-preserving local extension family** is

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t):=\{T\in\mathcal E(t):\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta\}.$$

Existence of members and the affine structure of these families require separate results; the set definitions alone assert neither.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by
$$ N_f=\{(f(x),\eta)\in T^*M\setminus0: df_x^T\eta=0\}. $$
If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$
For $u,v\in\mathcal D'(M)$, if there is no nonzero covector $\eta$ with both $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ at the same $x$, their product is defined by $uv=\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$, where $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$. It agrees with pointwise multiplication when $u,v$ are smooth and satisfies
$$ \operatorname{WF}(uv)\subseteq \{(x,\eta+\zeta):(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup0_M,\ (x,\zeta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup0_M,\ \eta+\zeta\ne0\}. $$
Here $0_M$ is the zero section. If $\pi:X\times Y\to X$ is a coordinate projection, $\nu$ is a smooth positive density on $Y$, and $t\in\mathcal E'(X\times Y)$, define $\pi_{*,\nu}t$ by
$$ \langle \pi_{*,\nu}t,\omega\rangle =\left\langle t,\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes\nu)\right\rangle, $$
where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$
The pullback condition is a local transversality requirement; this theorem does not define an arbitrary restriction of a singular kernel to a diagonal where the condition fails.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and let $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)$. Then there exists $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ such that $T|_U=t$ and $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta$. The result applies to arbitrary distributions with finite real scaling degree; it assumes no smooth kernel or pointwise product representation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $t\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta$, and let $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ be the set of its extensions in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ having scaling degree exactly $\delta$. This set is nonempty by [[thm-qft-finite-scaling-degree-extension]]. If $\delta<n$, then $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ has exactly one member. If $\delta\ge n$, let $k$ be the unique nonnegative integer with $k\le\delta-n<k+1$ (the floor of $\delta-n$). Then, for any $T_0\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$,

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t)=T_0+\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\partial^\alpha\delta_0:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$

Here a **point-local counterterm** means a distribution whose support, as defined in [[def-support-of-a-distribution]], is contained in $\{0\}$. Thus the same-degree freedom is finite dimensional, with precisely the displayed delta derivatives as its basis; at the threshold $\delta=n$, only a multiple of $\delta_0$ is allowed.

derivations.claim:
If $T$ has finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $d$, then for a multi-index $\alpha$,
$$\langle(\partial^\alpha T)_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\rho^{-|\alpha|}\langle T_\rho,\partial^\alpha\varphi\rangle.$$
Thus every exponent strictly above $\delta+|\alpha|$ makes the scaled derivative tend to zero, so $\operatorname{sd}_0(\partial^\alpha T)\le\delta+|\alpha|$. For a surjective linear map $L:\mathbb R^D\to\mathbb R^d$, choose linear coordinates $(y,w)$ with $y=Lx$ and $w\in\ker L$. The pullback $L^*T$ is $T(y)\otimes1(w)$ when it exists; integrating a test in $w$ shows the dilation factors $\rho^{-D}$ and the $w$-Jacobian $\rho^{D-d}$ cancel to the ordinary relative factor $\rho^{-d}$. Hence $\operatorname{sd}_0(L^*T)\le\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$.

For a wavefront-transversal pair $u,v$ on a resolved stratum, apply (PB) [A2] to obtain a finite-degree product and the bound $\operatorname{sd}_0(uv)\le\operatorname{sd}_0(u)+\operatorname{sd}_0(v)$. This step is exactly the extra product-scaling input; no conclusion that it follows from ordinary scaling degrees alone is used.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

The **Axiom of Countable Choice**, written $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$, is the following
statement.

> For every family $(X_n)_{n \in \mathbb{N}}$ of nonempty sets indexed by
> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

Equivalently, in the vocabulary of Choice function: every at most
countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.

In ZF,

$$\mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{DC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_\omega\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,\mathrm{fin}}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_{\omega,2},\qquad \mathrm{AC}\Longrightarrow\mathrm{AC}_2.$$

DC here includes a prescribed initial point.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and Countable Choice and fix admissible scalar free data as defined by the local time-ordered product contract. In addition assume the following product-scaling bound (PB): whenever two finite-scaling-degree distributions $u,v$ on one resolved causal stratum have a wavefront-transversal product, their product has finite relative scaling degree and
$$\operatorname{sd}_0(uv)\le\operatorname{sd}_0(u)+\operatorname{sd}_0(v).$$
Assume (PB) at every successive product of edge pullbacks and lower-order local counterterms used below. Fix a finite loopless multigraph $\Gamma$ with $n\ge2$ labeled vertices, parallel edges allowed, and a finite multi-index derivative $\alpha_e$ on each edge $e$. Suppose every proper partial-diagonal subgraph has already received an extension of finite scaling degree by induction on its number of vertices. Then the numerical graph distribution on the complement of the total diagonal has finite scaling degree in the $4(n-1)$ relative coordinates. For a primitive graph, with no proper divergent subgraph, the bound is
$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t_\Gamma)\le 2|E(\Gamma)|+\sum_{e\in E(\Gamma)}|\alpha_e|.$$
For a graph with proper subgraphs, the same induction gives a finite bound obtained from this edge estimate and the finitely many derivative orders of its lower-order local counterterms.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ have metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$, orientation $dx^0\wedge dx^1\wedge dx^2\wedge dx^3$, and future direction given by increasing $x^0$. Use units $c=1$, so a mass parameter has inverse-length units. Define $x\in J^+(y)$ by $x^0-y^0\ge|\mathbf x-\mathbf y|$ and $x\in J^-(y)$ by $y^0-x^0\ge|\mathbf y-\mathbf x|$; for $A\subseteq\mathbb M$, put $J^\pm(A)=\bigcup_{y\in A}J^\pm(y)$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi$; it is off shell because no field equation is imposed. The allowed local interactions are compactly supported finite polynomial functionals of $\phi$ and finitely many coordinate derivatives, integrated against $d^4x$. The support of a functional $F$ is the closed set of points each of whose neighborhoods contains the support of a compactly supported variation that changes $F$ for some configuration.

For $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$, require $\Lambda^{\mathsf T}\eta\Lambda=\eta$, $\det\Lambda=1$, and preservation of the chosen future cone; $SO^+(1,3)$ denotes this identity component. The proper orthochronous Poincare group consists of $\gamma=(a,\Lambda)$ with $a\in\mathbb M$ and $\Lambda\in SO^+(1,3)$. It acts by $(\gamma\cdot\phi)(x)=\phi(\Lambda^{-1}(x-a))$ and $(\gamma\cdot F)(\phi)=F(\gamma^{-1}\cdot\phi)$.

For a distribution on a coordinate chart, its wavefront set consists of the nonzero cotangent directions where every compact localization fails to have a rapidly decreasing Fourier transform in every conic neighborhood. Covectors are future or past causal when their metric-dual vectors are causal with the indicated time orientation; a nonzero causal covector has a nonzero time component. Write $\Delta=\{(x,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and $N^*\Delta=\{(x,\xi;x,-\xi):\xi\ne0\}$. Write $(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta)$ when $x,y$ lie on one null straight segment (a zero-length segment is allowed), and parallel transport along that segment carries $\xi$ to $\eta$. A fixed free scalar input consists of $m\ge0$, a two-point distribution $W$ satisfying
$$P_xW=P_yW=0,\qquad P=-\eta^{ab}\partial_a\partial_b+m^2,$$
and the positive-frequency null wavefront condition
$$\operatorname{WF}(W)=\mathcal C^+:=\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):(x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null}\}.$$
For a two-point distribution $U$, set $U^{\mathsf T}(x,y)=U(y,x)$ and let $U^*$ be complex conjugation. Assume $W$ is invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, satisfies $W-W^{\mathsf T}=iE$ for a fixed distribution $E$ supported where $x-y$ is causal, and satisfies $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$.

The prescribed scalar time-ordered contraction input is a symmetric distribution $H_F\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb M^2)$ invariant under translations and $SO^+(1,3)$, equal to $W(x,y)$ on the open set $x^0>y^0$ and to $W(y,x)$ on $y^0>x^0$. The two prescriptions agree on spacelike-separated open supports because $E$ is supported on causal pairs. Translation invariance gives $H_F(x,y)=h_F(x-y)$ and $W(x,y)=w(x-y)$. For a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^4$, set $T_\rho(\varphi)=\rho^{-4}T(\varphi(\cdot/\rho))$ and define $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)$ as the infimum of real $\omega$ for which $\rho^\omega T_\rho\to0$ on each fixed test as $\rho\downarrow0$. Require $\operatorname{sd}_0(h_F),\operatorname{sd}_0(w)\le2$ and
$$\operatorname{WF}(H_F)\subseteq\Gamma_F:=N^*\Delta\cup\{(x,\xi;y,-\eta):x\ne y,\ (x,\xi)\sim(y,\eta),\ \xi\text{ future null if }x\in J^+(y),\ \xi\text{ past null if }x\in J^-(y)\}.$$
This is fixed conditional data: it does not claim existence of $W$ or $H_F$, and it does not define any singular restriction or product of $H_F$ on a diagonal.

For $r\ge1$, $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ denotes the distribution kernel on $\mathbb M^r$ of the mixed variation in $r$ compactly supported smooth directions, and set $F^{(0)}(\phi)=F(\phi)$. Define $\deg F$ as the largest positive $r$ with $F^{(r)}\ne0$, or $0$ if all positive-order derivative kernels vanish; in particular $\deg0=0$. The class $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$ consists of finite polynomial functionals with compactly supported derivative kernels such that every nonzero wavefront tuple of each derivative kernel avoids both the cone of tuples whose entries are all future causal and the cone of tuples whose entries are all past causal; zero entries in either cone are allowed. For $F,G$ in this class, define
$$F\star_WG=\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)}\frac{\hbar^r}{r!}\left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle,$$
using distribution products and pushforwards under the stated wavefront transversality conditions, with the $r=0$ pairing interpreted as the pointwise product $F(\phi)G(\phi)$. Here $\hbar$ is a formal indeterminate, and Countable Choice is assumed for the supplier theorem defining these contractions.

A scalar time-ordered system is a sequence of symmetric multilinear maps
$$T_n:\big(\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\big)^n\longrightarrow \mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket,\qquad T_0=1,\quad T_1=\operatorname{id}.$$
For $I\subseteq\{1,\ldots,n\}$ put $S_I=\bigcup_{i\in I}\operatorname{supp}F_i$ and $F_I=(F_i)_{i\in I}$. Causal factorization requires
$$T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)=T_{|I|}(F_I)\star_W T_{|I^c|}(F_{I^c})$$
for every nonempty proper $I$ such that $S_I\cap J^-(S_{I^c})=\varnothing$; an empty block is the unit.

Field independence means that each numerical graph distribution is independent of the background field $\phi$; all $\phi$-dependence enters through the vertex kernels $F_i^{(r)}(\phi)$. In the graph expansion of $T_n$, vertices are labeled by $1,\ldots,n$ and an edge between distinct vertices contracts one derivative slot at each endpoint by $H_F$. A graph is a finite loopless multigraph, so parallel edges are allowed; if $r_{ij}$ edges join vertices $i$ and $j$, the Wick coefficient for that choice includes $\hbar^{\sum_{i<j}r_{ij}}/\prod_{i<j}r_{ij}!$. Finite-order local jet derivatives may act on incident edge kernels. Each coefficient is a finite sum of such contractions, since every input has finite polynomial degree. No graph term uses a singular product at a diagonal before extension.

For $n\ge2$, use relative coordinates $z_i=x_i-x_n$ ($1\le i<n$), so the total diagonal corresponds to $0\in\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}$. The relative scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma$ of a numerical graph distribution is defined by the same positive-dilation rule above in this relative dimension. The scaling condition requires each graph distribution on the punctured relative space, after its proper partial diagonals have been extended at lower vertex orders, to have a finite degree $\delta_\Gamma$, and each total-diagonal extension to retain that degree. Any two such extensions differ by derivatives $\partial^\beta\delta_0$ of order $|\beta|\le\lfloor\delta_\Gamma-4(n-1)\rfloor$ when $\delta_\Gamma\ge4(n-1)$, and agree when $\delta_\Gamma<4(n-1)$.

Covariance requires $T_n(\gamma\cdot F_1,\ldots,\gamma\cdot F_n)=\gamma\cdot T_n(F_1,\ldots,F_n)$ for each proper orthochronous Poincare transformation. Fix the Lorentz Lie-algebra convention $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_j$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_i$. For a formal coupling $g$, define coefficientwise
$$\mathcal S_g(V)=\sum_{n=0}^{\infty}\frac{(ig/\hbar)^n}{n!}T_n(V,\ldots,V).$$
The anti-time-ordered series is $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V):=\mathcal S_g(V)^*$, where the involution conjugates scalar coefficients, fixes real $g,\hbar$, and reverses the order of factors; $W^*=W^{\mathsf T}$ gives $(F\star_WG)^*=G^*\star_WF^*$. Formal unitarity requires $\overline{\mathcal S}_g(V)\star_W\mathcal S_g(V)=1$ for every real $V=V^*$. At each $g$-order, coefficients are finite Laurent polynomials in $\hbar$ before cancellation and are compared algebraically; there is no analytic convergence, positivity of formal coefficients, adiabatic limit, or gauge/Ward identity in this contract.

Let $\mathbb M=\mathbb R^4$ with coordinates $x=(x^0,x^1,x^2,x^3)$, metric $\eta=\operatorname{diag}(-1,1,1,1)$ and time orientation given by increasing $x^0$. A field configuration is any smooth real function $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$; it is off shell, meaning that it is not required to satisfy a field equation. For an integer $s\ge0$, its finite jet at $x$ is the finite tuple $j^s\phi(x)=(\partial^\alpha\phi(x))_{|\alpha|\le s}$, with multi-index derivatives in these coordinates.

An off-shell local polynomial scalar functional is a finite sum
$$F(\phi)=c+\sum_{a=1}^{N}\int_{\mathbb M} f_a(x)\,P_a(j^{s_a}\phi(x))\,d^4x,$$
where $c\in\mathbb C$, $f_a\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb C)$, each $P_a$ is a polynomial in the finitely many jet coordinates, and each $s_a$ is finite. Its support is contained in the compact set $\bigcup_{a=1}^{N}\operatorname{supp}f_a$. The collection of these functionals is denoted $\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$. The involution is $F^*(\phi)=\overline{F(\phi)}$. No physical units or field equation are imposed.

Precisely, $\operatorname{supp}F$ is the set of $x\in\mathbb M$ such that every neighborhood $U$ of $x$ contains the support of some $h\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ for which $F(\phi+h)\ne F(\phi)$ for some smooth configuration $\phi$. It is closed and is contained in the displayed compact union, so it is compact. This definition is independent of the chosen finite presentation of $F$.

For $r\ge1$, define the $r$th functional derivative by
$$F^{(r)}(\phi)(h_1,\ldots,h_r)=\left.\frac{\partial^r}{\partial t_1\cdots\partial t_r}F\!\left(\phi+\sum_{j=1}^{r}t_jh_j\right)\right|_{t_1=\cdots=t_r=0},\qquad h_j\in C_c^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R).$$
The finite polynomial expansion makes this a symmetric multilinear form. Repeated integration by parts in each $h_j$ writes it as a compactly supported distribution kernel on the thin diagonal $\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathbb M\}\subset\mathbb M^r$. Integrals use the fixed Minkowski density $d^4x$; all kernels are paired bilinearly with compactly supported smooth tests.

For every $F\in\mathcal F_{\mathrm{loc}}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$, every $\phi\in C^\infty(\mathbb M;\mathbb R)$ and every $r\ge1$, the kernel $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ satisfies
$$\operatorname{WF}(F^{(r)}(\phi))\subseteq N^*\Delta_r\setminus0,$$
where $\Delta_r=\{(x,\ldots,x):x\in\mathbb M\}$ and
$$N^*\Delta_r=\{(x,\ldots,x;\xi_1,\ldots,\xi_r):\xi_1+\cdots+\xi_r=0\}.$$
Consequently $F^{(r)}(\phi)$ avoids the all-future and all-past causal cotangent cones and $F$ belongs to $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(\mathbb M)$.

Assume $\mathrm{AC}_\omega$ and let $\hbar$ be a formal indeterminate. Let $W\in\mathcal D'(M\times M)$ be a scalar Hadamard bisolution. For $F,G\in\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)$, let $\deg F$ be the largest degree with nonzero coefficient kernel, with $\deg 0=0$, and define, coefficientwise in $\hbar$,
$$ F\star_W G =\sum_{r=0}^{\min(\deg F,\deg G)} \frac{\hbar^r}{r!} \left\langle F^{(r)}(\phi)\otimes G^{(r)}(\phi),\,W^{\otimes r}\right\rangle. $$
Each term is formed by the distribution product on the $r$ contracted variable pairs and proper pushforward over those pairs, as in [[thm-qftx-wavefront-product]], integrating with the metric density $\mu_g$ in each contracted variable. The sum is finite and defines a member of $\mathcal F_{\mu c}^{\mathrm{poly}}(M)\llbracket\hbar\rrbracket$. If $K\in C^\infty(M\times M)$ is symmetric, then
$$ \Gamma_KF(\phi)=\left\langle F^{(2)}(\phi),\chi K\mu_g^{\otimes2}\right\rangle $$
is also a compactly supported polynomial microcausal functional and lowers polynomial degree by two; here $\chi$ is any compactly supported cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}F^{(2)}(\phi)$.

Let $u\in\mathcal D'(M)$, where $M$ is a smooth manifold. For a smooth map $f:N\to M$, define its nonzero conormal set by
$$ N_f=\{(f(x),\eta)\in T^*M\setminus0: df_x^T\eta=0\}. $$
If $\operatorname{WF}(u)\cap N_f=\varnothing$, there is a distributional pullback $f^*u\in\mathcal D'(N)$ and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(f^*u)\subseteq \{(x,df_x^T\eta):(f(x),\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\}. $$
For $u,v\in\mathcal D'(M)$, if there is no nonzero covector $\eta$ with both $(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)$ and $(x,-\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)$ at the same $x$, their product is defined by $uv=\Delta^*(u\otimes v)$, where $\Delta(x)=(x,x)$. It agrees with pointwise multiplication when $u,v$ are smooth and satisfies
$$ \operatorname{WF}(uv)\subseteq \{(x,\eta+\zeta):(x,\eta)\in\operatorname{WF}(u)\cup0_M,\ (x,\zeta)\in\operatorname{WF}(v)\cup0_M,\ \eta+\zeta\ne0\}. $$
Here $0_M$ is the zero section. If $\pi:X\times Y\to X$ is a coordinate projection, $\nu$ is a smooth positive density on $Y$, and $t\in\mathcal E'(X\times Y)$, define $\pi_{*,\nu}t$ by
$$ \langle \pi_{*,\nu}t,\omega\rangle =\left\langle t,\chi(\pi^*\omega\otimes\nu)\right\rangle, $$
where $\omega$ is a compactly supported test density on $X$ and $\chi$ is a compact cutoff equal to one near $\operatorname{supp}t$. This pushforward is independent of $\chi$, compactly supported, and
$$ \operatorname{WF}(\pi_{*,\nu}t)\subseteq \{(x,\eta):\text{ for some }y,\ (x,y;\eta,0)\in\operatorname{WF}(t)\}. $$
The pullback condition is a local transversality requirement; this theorem does not define an arbitrary restriction of a singular kernel to a diagonal where the condition fails.

In ZF, for compact $K\subseteq\Omega\subseteq\mathbb R^n$ with $\Omega$ open, there is $\chi\in C_c^\infty(\Omega)$ with $0\le\chi\le1$ and $\chi=1$ on a neighborhood of $K$. Every open cover of $\Omega$ admits an at most countable locally finite smooth partition of unity with compact supports, each support contained in some cover member. Subordination here asserts existence of such a member for each support; it does not select cover labels.

In addition assume the following product-scaling bound (PB): whenever two finite-scaling-degree distributions $u,v$ on one resolved causal stratum have a wavefront-transversal product, their product has finite relative scaling degree and
$$\operatorname{sd}_0(uv)\le\operatorname{sd}_0(u)+\operatorname{sd}_0(v).$$

For a graph with proper subgraphs, the same induction gives a finite bound obtained from this edge estimate and the finitely many derivative orders of its lower-order local counterterms.

Fix an integer $n\ge1$, put $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and use the continuous complex-linear test-function pairing of [[def-distribution]]. For $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ and $\rho>0$, define its dilation at the origin by

$$\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle:=\rho^{-n}\langle t,\varphi(\cdot/\rho)\rangle,\qquad \varphi\in\mathcal D(U).$$

Positive dilations preserve $U$, so the displayed pairing is defined for every test function in $\mathcal D(U)$. If $t$ is the regular distribution induced by a locally integrable function $g$, change of variables gives $\langle t_\rho,\varphi\rangle=\int_U g(\rho x)\varphi(x)\,dx$.

Convergence $s_\rho\to0$ in $\mathcal D'(U)$ as $\rho\downarrow0$ means $\langle s_\rho,\varphi\rangle\to0$ for every fixed $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$. The **scaling degree at the origin** is

$$\operatorname{sd}_0(t):=\inf\{\omega\in\mathbb R:\rho^\omega t_\rho\to0\text{ in }\mathcal D'(U)\}.$$

The infimum of the empty set is $+\infty$; if every real $\omega$ belongs to the set, the infimum is $-\infty$. A finite scaling degree means a real value $\delta\in\mathbb R$. For a distribution $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ use the same dilation formula on tests in $\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$. An **extension** of $t$ is a distribution $T$ on $\mathbb R^n$ whose restriction to $U$ equals $t$. The degree of divergence associated with a finite scaling degree $\delta$ in dimension $n$ is $\delta-n$. Exact homogeneity of scaling degree $\delta$ means $\rho^\delta T_\rho=T$ for every $\rho>0$.

For this fixed $t$, define its **local extension family** by

$$\mathcal E(t):=\{T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n):T|_U=t\}.$$

Here $T|_U=t$ means $\langle T,\widetilde\varphi\rangle=\langle t,\varphi\rangle$ for every $\varphi\in\mathcal D(U)$, where $\widetilde\varphi\in\mathcal D(\mathbb R^n)$ is its smooth extension by zero. When $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)\in\mathbb R$, the **scaling-degree-preserving local extension family** is

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t):=\{T\in\mathcal E(t):\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta\}.$$

Existence of members and the affine structure of these families require separate results; the set definitions alone assert neither.

The definitions use Euclidean dilations about the specified point only. They do not assert that a given distribution arises from a product of fields or that an extension is physically selected.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, $U=\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\}$, and let $t\in\mathcal D'(U)$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta=\operatorname{sd}_0(t)$. Then there exists $T\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ such that $T|_U=t$ and $\operatorname{sd}_0(T)=\delta$. The result applies to arbitrary distributions with finite real scaling degree; it assumes no smooth kernel or pointwise product representation.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $n\ge1$, let $t\in\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n\setminus\{0\})$ have finite real scaling degree $\delta$, and let $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ be the set of its extensions in $\mathcal D'(\mathbb R^n)$ having scaling degree exactly $\delta$. This set is nonempty by [[thm-qft-finite-scaling-degree-extension]]. If $\delta<n$, then $\mathcal E_\delta(t)$ has exactly one member. If $\delta\ge n$, let $k$ be the unique nonnegative integer with $k\le\delta-n<k+1$ (the floor of $\delta-n$). Then, for any $T_0\in\mathcal E_\delta(t)$,

$$\mathcal E_\delta(t)=T_0+\operatorname{span}_{\mathbb C}\{\partial^\alpha\delta_0:|\alpha|\le k\}.$$

Here a **point-local counterterm** means a distribution whose support, as defined in [[def-support-of-a-distribution]], is contained in $\{0\}$. Let $\mathfrak l$ be the six-dimensional real Lie algebra with basis $J_1,J_2,J_3,K_1,K_2,K_3$ and brackets $[J_i,J_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, $[J_i,K_j]=\epsilon_{ijk}K_k$, and $[K_i,K_j]=-\epsilon_{ijk}J_k$, where $\epsilon_{ijk}$ is the alternating symbol with $\epsilon_{123}=1$. $$c([X,Y])=\rho(X)c(Y)-\rho(Y)c(X)\qquad(X,Y\in\mathfrak l),$$

then there is $v\in V$ such that $c(X)=\rho(X)v$ for every $X\in\mathfrak l$. No infinite-dimensional module, gauge cohomology, or interacting-field conclusion is asserted.

By [F6], after the already constructed proper subgraph extensions, each numerical coefficient $t_\Gamma$ on the punctured relative space $\mathbb R^{4(n-1)}\setminus\{0\}$ has a finite real scaling degree $\delta_\Gamma$.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> (Choice function).

there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

> $\mathbb{N}$ there is a function $f$ with domain $\mathbb{N}$ such that
> $f(n) \in X_n$ for every $n \in \mathbb{N}$.

countable family of nonempty sets has a choice function.
